---
title: "What is settled, and what is current work"
subtitle: "How much weight each quantity can carry"
---

A short guide to how much weight each quantity can carry.

## Ready to use

The per-opportunity quantities are the first ones to report: first differences on
the tie-presence scale, second differences for interactions, each split by creation
and maintenance margin, and averaged either at the observed waves or along
model-implied ministeps. The period-level contrast described below is the second,
and the two answer different questions rather than competing.

They are well defined, they are implemented, and their interpretation is the one
stated in Chapter 2: a probability change *per decision opportunity*, holding the
decision situation fixed.

Ego-level covariates are perturbed across the whole choice set rather than one
alternative at a time, for the reason given in the aside in Chapter 2. That happens
by itself, so the per-tie numbers you get for a sender effect are sound; they are
just a narrow summary of it. The probability-mass contrast is the fuller one, and it
is what to reach for before drawing conclusions about covariate sender effects.

## Comparability

Meta-analysing marginal effects rather than parameters is usually motivated by
some combination of five claims. They hold up differently, and two are worth
spelling out.

| claim | how it holds up |
|---|---|
| more meaningful than meta-analysing parameters | yes — a pooled coefficient averages quantities whose scales need not match |
| challenges "the same model for all networks" | yes, as a question worth asking rather than an answer already given |
| the exact same specification is less necessary | in part, and it rests on an assumption — below |
| the main advantage is a common scale | yes, though a common unit is not invariance — below |
| compare within networks, then those comparisons across networks | yes, and arguably the strongest of the five |

**On the specification.** Pooling probability-scale quantities is more forgiving
than pooling coefficients, since the numbers at least share units. But an effect
missing from one network's specification does not simply drop out: what a model
leaves unexplained is folded into everything else, so the remaining coefficients
contract and their AMEs move with them. Treating a non-estimable effect as a true
zero is an assumption about that network rather than something the scale provides —
reasonable where the effect really is negligible there, and worth stating rather
than leaving implicit.

**On the common scale.** The probability scale gives a common unit and an
interpretable quantity: the effective impact of a mechanism on decisions, in that
network's actual conditions. What it does not give is invariance. Where two
networks genuinely differ in how predictable their actors' decisions are, the same
underlying preference translates into different probability shifts — and an effect
size that comes out differently there is reporting something true. A difference in
AMEs identifies a difference in effective impact, noise included by construction;
it does not identify a difference in preferences.

## Over a whole period

Everything in Chapter 2 is per decision opportunity. A natural next question is what
a mechanism contributes over a whole period between two waves, and the quantity for
that is the **period-level tie probability contrast**: hold the counterfactual for
the whole period, follow the dyad's own tie probability along the model-implied
sequence, and difference the two endpoints.

Two things make it the one to report at the period level.

It absorbs the rate. Two networks whose actors decide at very different frequencies
can have the same per-opportunity effect and very different period-level pressure,
and only a period quantity reflects that — which is what makes comparison possible
when opportunity rates differ across the networks being compared.

And it stays a probability. The contrast is a difference between two probabilities
that a tie is present at the end of the period, so it is bounded in $[-1, 1]$ and
lives on the same scale as the thing you can observe: the difference in tie
proportions between one wave and the next. That is what lets the model-implied
number be set beside the observed one, which is the comparison Chapter 3 wanted and
could not have.

It is implemented and it is what Chapters 3 and 5 report. One limitation is worth
knowing. The recursion follows the focal tie's own two states and holds the mirror
tie fixed, so in a specification containing reciprocity the contrast understates
slightly — by a few percent in the cases examined, and by nothing at all where
reciprocity is absent.

## The rate parameter

Marginal effects for *rate effects themselves* sit outside everything above, and
that is a scope choice rather than an oversight: the rate governs how often an
actor is asked, which is a different kind of question from what the actor then
does, and giving it a probability-scale contrast of its own needs its own
treatment.

What is not a scope choice, and is easy to miss, is that the rate is already
inside one of the quantities above. A per-opportunity effect conditions on an
opportunity having arisen, so it holds tempo fixed and reports the mechanism net
of it. A period-level effect does not: how many chances a dyad gets is part of
what determines where it ends up, so tempo and choice are combined in the number
by construction. That is precisely why the period-level effect can be compared
across networks whose actors decide at different frequencies — and precisely why
it should not be read as a statement about preferences alone.

Which you want therefore depends on whether the tempo of a setting is part of
what you are comparing or something you would rather hold constant. Neither
answer is more correct in general, and a comparison is clearer if it says which
it has chosen. Where tempo differs a great deal between the networks being
compared — and in the classes studied here it differs more than anything else —
the choice does real work rather than none.

## Further reading

The SAOM itself is set out in @Snijders01 and, at book length, in @AMAND. For
marginal effects generally, @LongMustillo2021 is the closest thing to a standard
reference, and @Glasgow2022 covers the discrete-choice side. On the ERGM side,
@Duxbury2023 sets out the scaling problem and @Duxbury2026 develops effect sizes
for structural terms; @IndlekoferBrandes2013 is the nearest existing SAOM tool.
